messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Nabil is a 54-year-old married Arab American man who has spent most of his adult life as a community organizer, the kind of person who once moved comfortably through church basements, school auditoriums, and late evening neighborhood meetings, trusting that people could be rallied toward decency. The assault that brought him to treatment happened eight months ago, after an argument with his romantic partner in the partner’s apartment, a place Nabil had entered with the ease of someone who believed he was safe there. The attack turned physical in a darkened hallway near the bedroom after the lights had been switched off in the course of the fight. Nabil remembers being shoved into the wall, struck repeatedly, and trying to orient himself more by sound than sight. What has stayed with him most sharply are not complete images but flashes and noises: his partner’s breathing, the scrape of shoes, the low mechanical thudding from a helicopter passing overhead outside, all of it cut into disconnected pieces. He had trusted this man intimately, and in the weeks after, that betrayal came to dominate the way he understood what had happened: if someone he loved could turn on him there, then the world no longer worked by rules he recognized, and he took the fact that he had stayed in the relationship as proof that something about his own character had invited it.

Those conclusions gave particular force to the things that now set him off. Darkness is not simply unpleasant to him; it feels like the moment when trust failed and ordinary reality gave way. Passing the block where the apartment building stands, or even entering a similarly narrow hallway in one of the community centers where he works, can make him tense before he has consciously registered why. Aircraft sounds are especially potent. During evening canvassing events, when a helicopter circles overhead or a plane cuts low across the city, the sound seems to confirm his sense that danger can descend without warning, and almost instantly he is no longer fully in the present.

When this happens, the memory does not come back as a story. It arrives abruptly and whole in feeling but broken in form, as if he is dropped into fragments he cannot organize. He hears in his head what he heard that night—the pounding overhead, breath, movement in the dark—and for several seconds he struggles to place himself. Sometimes a dark stairwell after a neighborhood meeting will do it; sometimes just walking by the event site on his way to another appointment. The memory itself has made these cues feel broader and less predictable. Because it can be triggered without warning, he has come to experience whole categories of places and sounds as contaminated, always scanning for where the next jolt might come from.

Over the months, Nabil has tried to manage this by becoming relentlessly watchful around other people. At public meetings he positions himself near exits and studies faces as if danger might be legible in a glance or a shift in posture. He has altered his routes to avoid the street where the assault happened, even when that makes him late to organizing events. He has also started wearing loose jackets and long sleeves even in warm weather, wanting to draw less notice to himself, to feel less exposed. These habits make sense to him because the memories feel so immediate; if a place, a sound, or a moment of dim light can bring the assault back in full force, then staying alert and staying away seem like the only reasonable protections.

But those protections have deepened what he believes about himself and other people. Each time he crosses the street to avoid that block, or sits in the back of a meeting room measuring who might be dangerous, it leaves him feeling more certain that the world is fundamentally unsafe and that he has become the sort of man things happen to. The concealing clothing, meant to help him disappear, carries its own private shame; he reads his need for it as evidence of weakness. He has begun to think not only that he was betrayed, but that he should have known better, should have seen who this person really was, and that his failure to do so says something damning about his character.

At work this has narrowed his life. Nabil still shows up, but colleagues have noticed that he avoids evening events in unfamiliar buildings and resists campaigns that would place him near that neighborhood. If a helicopter passes during an outdoor gathering, he momentarily loses track of the conversation and scans the area, already bracing for the memory he fears is coming. That vigilance itself keeps the possibility of danger close; the more he searches people and places for signs of threat, the more readily darkness, certain streets, and overhead aircraft strike him as ominous.

He sought help after his wife told him that although he was physically present at home, he seemed to vanish whenever a sound or place caught him. What frightened him most was not only the memory of the beating, but the sense that it had rewritten his understanding of trust so completely that he might never move through the world normally again. What he hopes, quietly, is not to erase what happened, but to stop living as if every dark hallway, every familiar block, and every sound from the sky means it is happening again.
